narrative:
The model determined that you have a 95% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission based on predicted success, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the first decile (bottom 10%) of your class in Year 3 is far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking in the second decile also contributed to the negative outlook, though less dramatically, sitting well below the typical sixth-decile performance of admitted students.

Your family income bracket was the second most important factor. Being in the middle-income group slightly increased the predicted risk of failure compared with the large share of accepted students who come from upper-middle or high-income families.

Taken together, these academic performance signals and background factors created a clear picture for the model: a very high likelihood that the bar exam would not be passed on the first try. Gender and race played no role in this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or pursue further study, and consider targeted bar exam preparation programs that have strong first-time pass rates. Reapplying later with improved grades or a higher LSAT score could meaningfully change the prediction. (248 words)
